# What is `CLAUDE.md`?

`CLAUDE.md` is a Markdown file that lives at the root of a repository
and contains standing instructions for Claude Code. Every time you
start a session in that repository, Claude Code reads this file and
treats its contents as if you had pasted them into the conversation
yourself.

Think of it as: "I am tired of re-stating the same rules at the start
of every conversation. Just put them in this file and the assistant
will always know."

The file does three things for you:

1. **Encodes the strict session rules we developed in our chats**
   (source-of-truth discipline, no opportunistic fixes, ask before
   destructive operations, etc.) so they apply automatically.
2. **Documents project conventions** (file layout, roxygen style, the
   `base_args` API pattern, the AHR-vs-marginal-HR vocabulary) so
   you do not have to re-explain them each session.
3. **Establishes safety guardrails** (do not commit without approval,
   do not run long simulations without warning, do not bump
   DESCRIPTION versions silently) so the assistant cannot
   accidentally do something disruptive.

The file I have prepared for `forestsearch` does all three. It is
based directly on the rules and conventions that emerged from our
chat sessions over the past few months.

---

# Where to put it

The file goes at the **root of your `forestsearch` working tree** —
the same directory that contains `DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, `R/`,
`vignettes/`, etc.

```
forestsearch/
├── CLAUDE.md              ← here
├── DESCRIPTION
├── NAMESPACE
├── R/
├── vignettes/
├── tests/
└── ...
```

Not in `R/`, not in `vignettes/`, not in a subdirectory — root level.
Claude Code looks for `CLAUDE.md` in the working directory you launch
it from, walking up the directory tree if it does not find one there.

---

# Installing it: three steps

## Step 1 — Download the file

Use the `CLAUDE.md` artifact I provided alongside this document. Save
it to your machine — for instance, to your Downloads folder.

## Step 2 — Move it into the repository root

From a terminal:

```bash
cd ~/path/to/forestsearch     # adjust to your actual path
mv ~/Downloads/CLAUDE.md .
```

Or with a file-manager GUI: drag and drop into the `forestsearch`
folder.

Verify it landed in the right place:

```bash
ls -la CLAUDE.md
```

You should see the file listed at the root.

## Step 3 — Commit it (recommended)

```bash
git add CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Add CLAUDE.md with project rules for Claude Code"
```

This way the rules travel with the repository. If you ever work from
a different machine, the rules are already there. If a collaborator
joins, they get the same conventions.

If you would rather try the file out before committing, that is fine
— just be aware that uncommitted files can be accidentally deleted
by `git clean -fd` or similar operations.

---

# How to use it: from zero to a working session

The rest of this document is a worked example. I will walk you
through starting a session, doing one of the kinds of tasks we did
in chat, and pointing out where `CLAUDE.md` is silently doing the
work.

## Starting your first session

Open a terminal. Navigate to the repository:

```bash
cd ~/forestsearch
```

Launch Claude Code:

```bash
claude
```

You will see a prompt. The assistant has already read `CLAUDE.md` —
you do not need to mention it. A good first message is:

> *Confirm what branch I am on, summarise recent commits, and
> describe any uncommitted changes. Do not change anything yet.*

The assistant will run:

- `git status` — to see uncommitted changes
- `git log -10 --oneline` — to see recent commits
- `git branch --show-current` — to confirm the branch

And report back in plain language. You now have shared context.

**Why this matters.** In the chat sessions, the first thing I had to
do was figure out which version of which file we were working from.
With `CLAUDE.md` and a clean git status, that question is settled
before the conversation even begins.

## A worked example: adding `calibrate_k_treat()` to the package

This is the same task we did in our most recent chat session, but
now in Claude Code with the rules in place.

### Your prompt

> *I want to add a new exported function `calibrate_k_treat()` to
> the package. It should mirror the style of `calibrate_k_inter()`
> in `R/sim_aft_gbsg.R`. The function calibrates `k_treat` via
> `uniroot` so that the DGM's AHR (or marginal HR, controlled by a
> `use_ahr` flag) hits a target value. Please draft the function,
> write a smoke test, document the package, and confirm everything
> installs cleanly.*

### What Claude Code will do (with `CLAUDE.md` in place)

1. **Read `R/sim_aft_gbsg.R`** to learn `calibrate_k_inter()`'s
   style — roxygen format, parameter names, error messages,
   diagnostic output. (Rule 4: "Match the roxygen style of existing
   siblings.")

2. **Read `R/generate_aft_dgm_main.R`** to see the full signature of
   the constructor it will be wrapping. (Rule 4: "Functions
   wrapping `generate_aft_dgm_flex()` should accept a `base_args`
   named list.")

3. **Propose the new file path**: `R/calibrate_k_treat.R`. (Rule 4:
   "Functions live in `R/<name>.R`, one major exported function per
   file.") Ask for permission to create it.

4. **Draft the function** with the conventions encoded:
   - `base_args` parameter pattern, not `...`
   - `utils::modifyList()` for overrides, not `c()` (Rule 4: the
     specific duplicate-argument-error guidance we developed)
   - `verbose` flag emitting `message()` not `cat()`
   - `stopifnot()` for input validation
   - `warning()` if `base_args$seed` is `NULL`
   - Full roxygen including `@importFrom stats uniroot` and
     `@importFrom utils modifyList`

5. **Write `tests/testthat/test-calibrate_k_treat.R`** with a smoke
   test that builds a small GBSG DGM and confirms the calibrated
   function converges. (Rule 8: "For new exported functions,
   propose a smoke test that confirms the function runs end-to-end
   on a small example.")

6. **Run `Rscript -e 'devtools::document()'`** to regenerate the
   NAMESPACE entries for the new export. Wait for permission first
   if the install takes longer than ~30s. (Rule 9: "Do not run any
   operation that exceeds ~30 seconds of wall time without warning
   me first.")

7. **Run `Rscript -e 'devtools::install(quiet = TRUE)'`** to install
   the package locally with the new function.

8. **Run the smoke test** and report the calibrated `k_treat` value
   plus the achieved AHR and the target.

9. **Stop and ask** before committing. (Rule 7: "Propose commit
   messages but do not commit without explicit approval.")

This is roughly one Claude Code turn. In our chat sessions it took
five or six turns plus the back-and-forth of you running the smoke
test yourself.

### What the assistant will *not* do

- It will not "improve" `calibrate_k_inter()` while it has the file
  open. (Rule 2.)
- It will not bump the version in `DESCRIPTION`. (Rule 9.)
- It will not commit or push. (Rule 7.)
- It will not run a long simulation to "verify" beyond the smoke
  test. (Rule 9.)
- It will not silently fix any unrelated warnings it notices in
  related files. (Rule 2.)

These all came up as friction points in our chat sessions. The rules
encode the resolution we settled on.

# Three more worked examples

## Example A — Render and diagnose

Your prompt:

> *Render `vignettes/extreme_subgroups.qmd` and report any warnings
> or errors. Pay particular attention to the `build-dgm` chunk
> output and confirm the calibrated AHR matches 0.70 in the
> rendered HTML.*

What happens:

1. The assistant runs `quarto render vignettes/extreme_subgroups.qmd`.
2. Reads the resulting HTML directly off disk.
3. Greps for `cell-output-error` and `cell-output-stderr` blocks.
   (Rule 6: "After rendering, check the resulting HTML for
   `cell-output-error` and `cell-output-stderr` blocks and report
   any warnings or errors before declaring success.")
4. Extracts the calibration diagnostic text from the `build-dgm`
   chunk's output.
5. Reports findings.

If anything failed, the assistant has the actual stderr in hand and
can propose a fix in the same turn.

## Example B — Diagnose an unexpected number

Your prompt:

> *The mHR for the ITT row in the simulation results is 0.64, but
> the calibration reports overall HR = 0.70. Diagnose.*

What happens:

1. The assistant reads the relevant qmd chunks to understand what
   `dgm_uniform$hazard_ratios$overall`, `$AHR`, and the simulation
   Cox spec actually are.
2. Notices the distinction between marginal Cox HR and AHR (Rule 5
   makes this an explicit project concept, so the assistant will
   spot it).
3. Writes a short probe script that builds the DGM, prints both HR
   summaries, and simulates 100 trials to compare the stratified
   Cox HR median.
4. Runs the probe.
5. Reports the three numbers and explains the gap as Cox
   non-collapsibility.
6. Proposes the fix: `use_ahr = TRUE` in the
   `calibrate_k_treat()` call. (Rule 5: "Calibration targets the
   AHR by default because the simulation Cox is
   stratified-by-grade.")

You see the diagnosis with actual numbers, not handwaving. This is
the loop that took us several chat turns to work through.

## Example C — Iterating on a table layout

Your prompt:

> *The "All Parameters" table in `fsparams_summary.qmd` is too wide
> and the columns look mis-aligned in the rendered HTML. Please
> render it, look at the output, and suggest improvements. Apply
> them and iterate with me.*

What happens:

1. The assistant renders `fsparams_summary.qmd`.
2. Reads the resulting HTML and identifies the layout issues (column
   count, value formatting, missing alignment).
3. Proposes 3–4 concrete improvements as a numbered list with a
   recommendation. (Rule 3: "When proposing multiple options,
   present them as a short numbered list with a clear
   recommendation.")
4. You pick which to apply.
5. The assistant applies them and re-renders.
6. You react. Loop until satisfied.

This loop in chat took us four uploads of HTML files and four
rounds of patching. With Claude Code it is one continuous
conversation.

# What to do if something goes wrong

## Claude Code did something I did not want

Use git to revert. If you committed before the session:

```bash
git status                       # see what was touched
git diff                         # see the changes
git restore <file>               # revert specific file
git restore .                    # revert all uncommitted changes
```

If you did *not* commit before the session, the safety net is
weaker. This is why I strongly recommend a clean `git status` before
launching `claude`.

## Claude Code seems confused about which file to edit

`CLAUDE.md` Rule 1 should prevent this, but if it slips:

> *Stop. State which file you are about to edit, with the full path
> from the repo root. Confirm the version you are reading is the
> on-disk version, not a stale view from earlier in this session.*

This forces the assistant to re-anchor.

## A command is taking forever

Cancel with Ctrl-C. The assistant will report what was canceled.
Then ask it to break the task into smaller pieces. (Rule 9 should
prevent this happening unprompted, but if you ask for a long
simulation directly, the rule does not block you.)

## The assistant disagreed with you

`CLAUDE.md` Rule 3 says honest disagreement is welcome. If the
assistant pushes back on a proposed change, take it seriously —
that exchange is doing real work. Ask for the reasoning. If you
still want to proceed, you can, but consider whether the objection
identified a real issue.

## You want to override the rules for one session

You can. Just say so:

> *For this session only, please ignore Rule 7 and commit changes
> directly without asking. I am doing a bulk cleanup and approving
> every commit individually is too slow.*

The assistant will acknowledge and adjust. The rules are guidance,
not a straitjacket.

---

# Editing the rules over time

`CLAUDE.md` is not set in stone. As you work with Claude Code you
will discover new conventions you want encoded — or rules that turn
out to be annoying in practice.

Edit the file directly. Commit the changes. The next session will
pick up the new rules.

Good triggers for updates:

- You found yourself re-stating the same instruction at the start of
  three different sessions. Encode it.
- The assistant did something disruptive that a rule would have
  prevented. Add the rule.
- A convention you set up months ago no longer applies. Remove or
  update it.

Treat `CLAUDE.md` like any other piece of project documentation: a
living artifact that gets refined as the project evolves.

---

# A minimal session checklist

Print this and tape it next to your terminal, at least for the
first few sessions:

1. **Working directory clean.** `git status` shows no uncommitted
   changes, or only changes you are aware of.
2. **Branch correct.** `git branch --show-current` is what you
   expect.
3. **Launch.** `cd ~/forestsearch && claude`.
4. **First message: orient.** "Confirm branch, recent commits, any
   uncommitted changes. Do not change anything yet."
5. **State your goal clearly.** "I want to do X. The acceptance
   criterion is Y."
6. **Review permission prompts.** Read what is being asked before
   approving.
7. **Stop and commit at logical milestones.** Use git as your save
   point.
8. **End the session deliberately.** Ctrl-D or `exit`.

Five sessions of this and it will feel automatic.

---

# Frequently asked questions

**Do I have to have `CLAUDE.md` to use Claude Code?**

No. Claude Code works without it — but you will end up restating
the same rules at the start of every session. The file is a
convenience.

**Does `CLAUDE.md` apply to the web chat too?**

No. The web chat does not read this file. The rules in `CLAUDE.md`
parallel the strict session rules we developed in our chat
sessions, but they are encoded specifically for Claude Code.

**Can I have different `CLAUDE.md` files for different projects?**

Yes. Each repository has its own. The conventions for
`forestsearch` (R package, Quarto vignettes, AHR vocabulary) are
different from what you might want for, say, a Python data-analysis
project.

**What if I want one rule to apply everywhere I use Claude Code?**

There is a separate user-level configuration file (consult the
official docs at [claude.com/claude-code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
for the exact path on your operating system). Rules placed there
apply to every session regardless of repository. `CLAUDE.md` is for
project-specific rules.

**Will Claude Code respect every rule perfectly?**

Mostly, yes. Occasionally a rule and a specific instruction will be
in tension, and the assistant will use judgement. If it does the
wrong thing, point it out — and consider whether the rule needs to
be sharpened.

**Can I share `CLAUDE.md` with other contributors to the package?**

Yes, and you should. That is one of the reasons to commit it to the
repository. Anyone who clones the repo and uses Claude Code gets
the same conventions automatically.
